title: Add to your faith (2 Peter 1:5–8)
hook: a ladder: faith, virtue, knowledge, self-control, patience, godliness, kindness, love
tomorrow: who keeps you from falling when you can't keep yourself?

segments.voice: Cast your cares, because he cares for you, and stay awake while you do. The worry got thrown. Now the question is what to build once it's gone.
screen: `HE CARES FOR YOU.` → `WHAT DO YOU BUILD NEXT?`

segments.voice: In a martial arts gym, the white belt isn't a failure. It's where everyone starts, and nobody expects you to stay there. Is faith the finish line, or only the first step? A short letter called Second Peter answers with a list that climbs like belts: "Add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge." And it keeps going, rung on rung. Faith, in this letter, is the white belt.
screen: `THE WHITE BELT.` → `FINISH LINE OR FIRST STEP?` → `ADD TO YOUR FAITH.`

segments.voice: Today's question: what does a good life grow? Here's the whole climb, in the King James: "giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge; And to knowledge temperance; and to temperance patience; and to patience godliness; And to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness charity." Virtue is goodness that does something. Temperance is self-control. Patience is staying power. And at the top, charity: love. The verses just before say God's power has already given "all things that pertain unto life and godliness." So the gift comes first, and the climb answers it, with real effort. A neighbor tradition keeps a list like this too. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna the marks of a person born to a divine nature: fearlessness, generosity, self-control, truthfulness, freedom from anger, compassion for all beings, gentleness, forgiveness, steadiness. What's shared is the shape: a good life isn't one feeling, it's qualities grown side by side, self-control and gentleness among them. And the honest difference: Second Peter's ladder stands on faith in Christ and climbs to love at the top. The Gita's list belongs to Krishna's teaching on two natures and the path toward freedom. Different ground, different summit. Some of the same rungs.
screen: `FAITH IS THE FIRST RUNG.` · `THE GIFT FIRST, THEN THE CLIMB.` · `THE GITA'S LIST: A NEIGHBOR.` · `SOME SAME RUNGS, DIFFERENT SUMMIT.` · then, large: `ADD TO YOUR FAITH.`

segments.voice: Run through the rungs: virtue, knowledge, self-control, patience, godliness, kindness, love, and pick the one that seems next for you. Name the wish: one real step on that rung. Name what usually trips you there. Then decide on one small thing you'll do the moment that obstacle shows up.
Add to your faith. Second Peter, chapter one: a climb from faith through virtue, knowledge and patience, all the way up to love.
Your line: add to your faith. The first rung is a start, not a finish. Go gently.

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3. Title, word, carry and sources kept; Bhagavad Gita 16:1–3 added for the unity thread. The KJV 'neither barren nor unfruitful' (1:8) moved from the voice to the trapdoor, cited as a paraphrase.

v3 wisdom shape and unity thread (owner, 'more alike than we think'): Bhagavad Gita 16:1–3 paraphrased, not quoted (Arnold 1885 is public domain, but its wording was not verified here). The paraphrase selects from the list (abhayam fearlessness, danam generosity, damah self-control, satyam truthfulness, akrodhah freedom from anger, daya bhuteshu compassion for beings, mardavam gentleness, kshama forgiveness, dhritih steadiness/fortitude) and does not claim to be the whole list. Shared: a good life as qualities grown side by side, with self-control and gentleness on both lists. Honest difference: 2 Peter's ladder stands on faith in Christ and climbs to love; the Gita's list belongs to Krishna's teaching on the divine and demonic natures (Gita 16) and the path toward liberation. 'Different ground, different summit' ranks neither. Confirm with a Christian Keeper and, ideally, a Hindu reader; confirm 'Krishna, God' in the gloss is how the Gita's readers would put it (many Hindus understand Krishna as God; some traditions as an avatar of Vishnu).

The short definitions of each rung (virtue as goodness that acts, temperance as self-control, patience as staying power) are plain glosses of the KJV words; please confirm. No count of the rungs is given.

The chat's wrong option ('working at something means you don't trust God') is a misreading of 2 Peter 1:5's 'giving all diligence', not a church's teaching; no church's view of faith and works is set up as the wrong answer. Confirm the tone.
The hook's white-belt picture is the writer's illustration.
